column3: Near-exact parallel: one cry leaves all gathered and brought before Us.
Universal creation and guardianship supports the focus ayah's all-inclusive divine summons.
Complete angelic unanimity offers only a formal parallel to universal totality.
Every soul's guardian supplies an individual-accountability frame for the focus's collective presentation.
The preceding rejection of messengers helps situate the warning that follows in the same passage.
Each soul knowing what it has brought clarifies presentation as an evidentiary encounter.
The boast of a united victorious group is a limited, worldly use of collective language.
The immediate antecedent contrasts perished generations' non-return with their eventual presentation before God.
It explicitly names God as gatherer of all people for an undoubted Day.
It repeats the angelic unanimity already supplied by 38:73 without adding judgment or presentation.
The mass emergence of Gog and Magog offers a distant image of movement from every height.
Every soul finds its good and evil deeds made present, adding the content of accountability.
With Us introduces stored punishment but does not explain the gathering of all people.
Reviving dead earth begins the passage's local signs that support resurrection.
Its universal warning against every slanderer does not clarify gathering or presentation.
The Book's being with God is a different use of presence.
The differentiation of every wise matter is too general to explain persons being presented.
Being among those brought forth shows presentation as an avoided punitive outcome.
It states that every person receives full recompense for deeds, specifying the focus's judgment horizon.
The gardens and springs continue the earthly-sign passage without adding to the focus ayah.
It contrasts fulfillment of a good promise with being brought forth on the Day of Resurrection.
Those resisting the signs are brought into punishment, supplying one consequence of presentation.
A command issuing from God is not the collective presence described in the focus ayah.
God can gather dispersed creatures whenever He wills, directly linking dispersion and reassembly.
A mustered army unable to help its gods is a narrower, ironic form of being made present.
Human origin from a drop supports the surrounding argument that resurrection is possible.
Its contrast is between divine mercy and worldly accumulation, not eschatological gathering.
Being established in the king's presence is unrelated to universal presentation before God.
Universal measured creation provides a remote premise for an ordered comprehensive judgment.
It directly sequences life, death, and gathering to the undoubted Day of Resurrection.
It identifies disbelievers as brought into punishment after denying the Hereafter.
The objection about decayed bones articulates the resurrection question answered by the surrounding passage.
God's witness over everything is a broad accountability premise rather than a gathering scene.
It contrasts transient worldly possessions with the Hereafter being with the Lord.
Iblis's absence from the worshippers adds no further insight beyond the prior angelic scene.
The collective mention of favored prophets is unrelated to eschatological assembly.
It combines diverse communities' paths with everyone's return to God and disclosure of disputes.
The first Creator's knowledge of every creation answers how decayed bones can live again.
It calls the Last Day one for which people are gathered and witnessed.
Attendance at allotted turns of water is not the final presentation of all.
Created pairs do not illuminate resurrection, judgment, or presence before God.
The totality of creation being subjected to humanity is only a broad counterpart to "all."
Hostile looks and accusation do not concern gathering or final accountability.
Fire drawn from a green tree supports the local argument from unexpected transformation to resurrection.
It depicts the comprehensive filling of Hell with Iblis and all his followers.
Innumerable blessings and human ingratitude do not add to the focus ayah.
Allocated portions at Hell's gates give a limited picture of ordered punitive sorting.
Summoning every skilled magician is a worldly assembly with no final-judgment connection.
God's power over everything is a general premise but adds no specific gathering or presentation.
The Creator of heavens and earth is explicitly able to recreate their like, advancing the passage's resurrection proof.
Doubt about meeting the Lord directly addresses the encounter presupposed by being presented before Him.
A group's claim to be collectively vigilant has no eschatological relevance.
The totality of messenger reports serves consolation, not collective resurrection or judgment.
All inhabitants of Hell acknowledge that God has judged between His servants.
It applies the same brought-forth formula to deniers, confirming its punitive judicial force.
The immediate context shows the destroyed town needing no heavenly army, before the passage generalizes the fate of generations.
The creation of all pairs concerns cosmological ordering, not the final assembly.
It makes Hell the appointed meeting-place for all who follow the devil.
Iblis's refusal of the angelic worship does not add beyond the earlier parallel.
It preserves distinct membership and kinship claims under God's comprehensive knowledge.
God doing what He wills is too general to add to the focus ayah.
The immediate predecessor's single cry and their extinction form the local transition to all being presented.
Everyone in heavens and earth belongs to God and is devoted to Him.
The diversity of human striving does not explain their later gathering.
The trumpet sends people from graves hastening toward their Lord, directly preceding the universal presentation.
People and devils are gathered and brought kneeling around Hell, a detailed punitive presentation scene.
The incomplete statement supplies no substantive link to the focus ayah.
Chained criminals portray collective punishment but not their gathering before God.
Provision and divine knowledge are unrelated to resurrection or presentation.
God's collection and recitation concern preserving revelation, not gathering people.
The resurrected recognize the Merciful's promise, immediately explaining the event before 36:53.
Past destruction of all wrongdoers is not itself final presentation.
It explicitly gathers them for an undoubted Day and fully repays every soul without injustice.
Iblis claims he will mislead all, but the statement is qualified by the following exception.
Creation of all that is on earth offers only a broad divine-capacity premise.
God raises all people, informs them of their deeds, and has counted what they forgot.
The same surah joins raising the dead with recording every deed in a clear register.
Grouping named prophets among the good does not bear on final assembly.
The denial of the promised event supplies the skeptical counterpart to its fulfillment in the focus ayah.
Fruit at every season is an unrelated use of universality.
A set of prohibited acts being disliked by God does not explain presentation.
The rescue of Moses and his followers is a limited historical collective, not final gathering.
Divine ownership and the Hour's loss for falsifiers provide only a general judgment setting.
Hoarding gathered wealth is unrelated to people being gathered before God.
Despite differing directions, God will bring everyone together wherever they are.
The command for angels to prostrate is remote from eschatological presentation.
Its universal description of deniers does not add to gathering or judgment.
Successive communities are all brought together in the Fire while retaining shared and individual responsibility.
Iblis's refusal repeats the earlier angelic episode without advancing the focus theme.
Providing every kind of example in the Quran is unrelated to final assembly.
The descent upon each sinful liar has no connection to the focus ayah.
It leaves disputed claims for God to gather the parties and bring them to the final return.
Excellence in every created thing is not a specific resurrection or judgment link.
Every soul is recompensed for what it earned, preserving individual judgment within the collective scene.
Divine ownership of heaven and earth adds no distinct insight after stronger universal premises.
The guarded highest assembly is unrelated to humanity's final presentation.
It describes Hell being filled with all jinn and humans in a comprehensive punitive outcome.
God gathers all and then interrogates alleged partners, making presentation an explicit accountability scene.
Human development and reviving dead earth directly answer doubt about resurrection.
It contrasts divine grace with amassed worldly goods, not final gathering.
The immediate continuation makes the presentation judicial: no soul is wronged and each is repaid for its deeds.
God gathers all people and leaves not one of them behind, making the focus ayah's totality explicit.
All are set in ranks before their Lord and confronted with their return as first created.
On the Day God gathers all, alleged partners and their worshippers are separated for interrogation.
The changed earth and heavens culminate in all people emerging before the One, the Irresistible.
It answers doubt about re-creation by naming the original Creator and the Day He calls all people.
The divine call brings people forth praising God, while their worldly stay appears brief.
The trumpet is blown and all are gathered together in one complete gathering.
Remembering humanity's first creation supplies a direct premise for re-creation after death.
Humanity is created from earth, returned to it, and brought out again.
All follow the Caller without deviation, portraying the inescapable movement to final presence.
Faces are humbled before the Ever-Living, Sustainer, specifying the posture of presentation.
The first creation is repeated when the heavens are rolled up, grounding return in divine creative power.
The certain Hour entails God raising all who are in the graves.
Death is followed by resurrection on the Day of Resurrection.
It explicitly states that all will be raised on the Day of Resurrection.
The trumpet suspends worldly kinship claims, emphasizing the individual final encounter.
Gathering a group from every nation for the signs is a partial, rather than universal, assembly.
The trumpet's sounding places every creature in the heavens and earth under divine awe.
God originates creation and then repeats it, after which all are returned to Him.
Creating and resurrecting all humanity is likened to creating and resurrecting one soul.
God gathers the disputing parties and judges between them in truth.
One cry brings them forth looking on, closely paralleling the event in the focus passage.
Those brought forth are stopped for questioning, adding the judicial purpose of presence.
The trumpet ends the first order and then leaves all standing and looking after resurrection.
The earth is illuminated, records and witnesses are brought, and judgment is rendered without injustice.
Every soul receives full recompense for what it did, completing the focus's presentation with judgment.
On that Day every soul is repaid for what it earned, with no injustice under God's swift reckoning.
The Day of Decision is the appointed time for all, framing the universal gathering as adjudication.
Every community is seen kneeling and called to its record, a collective presentation joined to documentation.
The record speaks truth about what people did, defining the evidence used in final judgment.
The trumpet marks the arrival of the promised Day.
Every soul comes with a driver and witness, a precise picture of compelled presentation.
The lifted veil makes the final encounter fully visible to the person concerned.
The true cry is heard on the Day people emerge from the graves.
People emerge from graves with humbled eyes, moving like scattered locusts toward the Caller.
The earliest and latest generations are gathered for a known appointed Day.
It confirms that all generations are assembled at that appointed meeting.
God raises all people and exposes how their false oaths fail before Him.
Those denying resurrection are told they will certainly be raised and informed of what they did.
On the Day of presentation no hidden secret remains concealed.
People emerge from graves hastening as though toward erected markers.
Humbled eyes and abasement identify this emergence as the promised Day.
The Day of Decision is fixed as an appointed time.
The trumpet is blown and all people come in crowds.
A single cry brings people suddenly to awareness, a brief parallel to the focus event.
When graves are scattered, their opening supplies the resurrection setting.
It challenges the denial that people will be raised.
People stand before the Lord of all worlds on the great Day.
Every human toils toward the Lord and will meet Him.
People issue forth in scattered groups to be shown their deeds, linking resurrection to disclosure.
